title: USMLE Step 1: Microbiology

sources.name: Original educational wording based on standard microbiology knowledge
NCBI Bookshelf: bacterial structure (selected fact checks)

description: For medical learners reviewing bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, and microbial mechanisms for Step 1. Educational review only; verify with current guidelines.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Staphylococcus aureus?
cards.back: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase-positive and coagulase-positive.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Staphylococcus aureus?
cards.back: Skin abscesses, bacteremia, endocarditis, and toxin-mediated food poisoning are classic associations.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Staphylococcus epidermidis?
cards.back: Coagulase-negative staphylococcus that forms biofilms on implanted material.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Staphylococcus epidermidis?
cards.back: Prosthetic-device infections; it can also contaminate blood cultures from skin flora.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Staphylococcus saprophyticus?
cards.back: Coagulase-negative staphylococcus classically resistant to novobiocin in laboratory identification.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Staphylococcus saprophyticus?
cards.back: Urinary tract infection, especially in young sexually active women.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Streptococcus pyogenes?
cards.back: Group A, beta-hemolytic streptococcus with M protein as a major virulence factor.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Streptococcus pyogenes?
cards.back: Pharyngitis, impetigo, invasive soft-tissue infection, and postinfectious immune complications.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Streptococcus agalactiae?
cards.back: Group B, beta-hemolytic streptococcus; classically CAMP-test positive.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Streptococcus agalactiae?
cards.back: Neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis, often acquired around delivery.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Streptococcus pneumoniae?
cards.back: Encapsulated, alpha-hemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococci; classically optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Streptococcus pneumoniae?
cards.back: Community-acquired pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, and sinusitis.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Viridans streptococci?
cards.back: A heterogeneous group of oral streptococci, often alpha-hemolytic and optochin-resistant.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Viridans streptococci?
cards.back: Dental caries for some species and subacute infective endocarditis after entry into blood.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Streptococcus gallolyticus?
cards.back: A group D streptococcus historically included in the S. bovis group.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Streptococcus gallolyticus?
cards.back: Bacteremia or endocarditis has an important association with colorectal neoplasia.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Enterococcus faecalis?
cards.back: Gram-positive enteric coccus; can grow in bile and high-salt media.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Enterococcus faecalis?
cards.back: Urinary tract infection, endocarditis, and infections associated with healthcare exposure.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Enterococcus faecium?
cards.back: Enteric gram-positive coccus often showing greater antimicrobial resistance than E. faecalis.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Enterococcus faecium?
cards.back: Healthcare-associated bacteremia and other opportunistic infections.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Bacillus anthracis?
cards.back: Large, spore-forming gram-positive rod with a poly-D-glutamate capsule; typically nonmotile.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Bacillus anthracis?
cards.back: Anthrax, including a painless cutaneous lesion with a black eschar or severe inhalational disease.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Bacillus cereus?
cards.back: Motile, spore-forming gram-positive rod producing emetic or diarrheal toxins.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Bacillus cereus?
cards.back: Foodborne illness; the emetic syndrome is classically associated with improperly stored cooked rice.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Clostridium tetani?
cards.back: Anaerobic spore-forming rod producing tetanospasmin.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Clostridium tetani?
cards.back: Tetanus causes spastic paralysis by blocking release of inhibitory neurotransmitters.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Clostridium botulinum?
cards.back: Anaerobic spore-forming rod producing botulinum neurotoxin.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Clostridium botulinum?
cards.back: Botulism causes descending flaccid paralysis through impaired acetylcholine release.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Clostridium perfringens?
cards.back: Anaerobic spore-forming rod with an alpha toxin that acts as a phospholipase.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Clostridium perfringens?
cards.back: Myonecrosis with gas production and a separate enterotoxin-mediated foodborne illness.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Clostridioides difficile?
cards.back: Anaerobic spore-forming rod whose major toxins injure colonic epithelial cells.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Clostridioides difficile?
cards.back: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Clostridium septicum?
cards.back: Anaerobic spore-forming rod capable of invasive soft-tissue disease.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Clostridium septicum?
cards.back: Spontaneous myonecrosis has an association with colorectal malignancy and neutropenia.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Listeria monocytogenes?
cards.back: Facultatively intracellular gram-positive rod with tumbling motility and actin-based cell-to-cell spread.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Listeria monocytogenes?
cards.back: Neonatal infection and meningitis in older or immunocompromised people; important in pregnancy.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
cards.back: Club-shaped gram-positive rod; toxigenic strains carry a phage-encoded toxin.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
cards.back: Diphtheria can cause a pharyngeal pseudomembrane, myocarditis, and neuropathy.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Cutibacterium acnes?
cards.back: Anaerobic gram-positive rod that normally inhabits skin follicles.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Cutibacterium acnes?
cards.back: Acne and some implanted-device infections.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Actinomyces israelii?
cards.back: Branching, filamentous, anaerobic gram-positive bacterium; not acid-fast.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Actinomyces israelii?
cards.back: Cervicofacial abscesses and draining sinus tracts with sulfur granules.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Nocardia species?
cards.back: Aerobic branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Nocardia species?
cards.back: Pulmonary infection and brain abscess, especially with impaired cell-mediated immunity.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
cards.back: Acid-fast rod with a mycolic-acid-rich envelope; an intracellular pathogen of macrophages.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
cards.back: Tuberculosis, which may be pulmonary, latent, or disseminated.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Mycobacterium leprae?
cards.back: Acid-fast organism with tropism for cooler tissues and peripheral nerves; not grown on routine artificial media.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Mycobacterium leprae?
cards.back: Leprosy, with skin lesions and peripheral neuropathy across a spectrum determined by host immunity.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Mycobacterium avium complex?
cards.back: Environmental nontuberculous mycobacteria.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Mycobacterium avium complex?
cards.back: Disseminated disease in advanced immunosuppression and pulmonary disease in susceptible hosts.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Neisseria meningitidis?
cards.back: Encapsulated gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose and maltose.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Neisseria meningitidis?
cards.back: Meningitis and meningococcemia, sometimes with purpura and shock.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
cards.back: Gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose but not maltose; lacks a conventional polysaccharide capsule.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
cards.back: Urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and disseminated infection.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Moraxella catarrhalis?
cards.back: Oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus of the respiratory tract.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Moraxella catarrhalis?
cards.back: Otitis media, sinusitis, and exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Haemophilus influenzae?
cards.back: Small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus requiring X and V growth factors.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Haemophilus influenzae?
cards.back: Respiratory disease; encapsulated type b can cause invasive disease such as meningitis and epiglottitis.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Bordetella pertussis?
cards.back: Gram-negative coccobacillus whose pertussis toxin increases cellular cAMP by modifying Gi.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Bordetella pertussis?
cards.back: Pertussis, with paroxysmal cough; young infants may present with apnea.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Legionella pneumophila?
cards.back: Intracellular gram-negative organism associated with water systems; grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Legionella pneumophila?
cards.back: Pneumonia with possible gastrointestinal symptoms and hyponatremia; exposure is often from contaminated aerosols.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
cards.back: Oxidase-positive, nonfermenting gram-negative rod producing pigments including pyocyanin.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
cards.back: Opportunistic pneumonia, burn-wound infection, and infection in people with cystic fibrosis.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Escherichia coli?
cards.back: Lactose-fermenting gram-negative enteric rod; strains differ substantially in virulence factors.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Escherichia coli?
cards.back: Urinary tract infection, sepsis, neonatal meningitis, and several distinct diarrheal syndromes.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Klebsiella pneumoniae?
cards.back: Encapsulated, nonmotile, lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Klebsiella pneumoniae?
cards.back: Pneumonia, urinary infection, and bacteremia; some hypervirulent strains cause liver abscess.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Proteus mirabilis?
cards.back: Motile gram-negative rod with swarming growth and urease activity.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Proteus mirabilis?
cards.back: Urinary infections and struvite stones promoted by urine alkalinization.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Salmonella Typhi?
cards.back: Human-adapted motile gram-negative enteric pathogen with Vi capsular antigen.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Salmonella Typhi?
cards.back: Enteric fever; chronic carriage can involve the gallbladder.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Nontyphoidal Salmonella?
cards.back: Motile gram-negative enteric bacteria commonly associated with animal reservoirs.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Nontyphoidal Salmonella?
cards.back: Gastroenteritis and sometimes invasive disease; osteomyelitis is an association in sickle cell disease.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Shigella species?
cards.back: Nonmotile gram-negative enteric bacteria with a low infectious dose.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Shigella species?
cards.back: Inflammatory or bloody diarrhea from invasion of colonic mucosa.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Yersinia enterocolitica?
cards.back: Gram-negative coccobacillus that can grow at low temperatures.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Yersinia enterocolitica?
cards.back: Enterocolitis and mesenteric adenitis that can mimic appendicitis.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Yersinia pestis?
cards.back: Gram-negative coccobacillus associated with rodent reservoirs and flea transmission.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Yersinia pestis?
cards.back: Plague, including bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic forms.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Vibrio cholerae?
cards.back: Curved, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod whose cholera toxin activates Gs signaling.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Vibrio cholerae?
cards.back: Profuse watery diarrhea caused by increased intestinal fluid secretion.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Vibrio vulnificus?
cards.back: Halophilic gram-negative organism associated with coastal water and raw seafood.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Vibrio vulnificus?
cards.back: Severe wound infections and sepsis, especially in people with chronic liver disease.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Campylobacter jejuni?
cards.back: Curved gram-negative rod that grows in microaerophilic conditions, often at 42 degrees Celsius.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Campylobacter jejuni?
cards.back: Inflammatory diarrhea; subsequent Guillain-Barré syndrome or reactive arthritis may occur.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Helicobacter pylori?
cards.back: Curved, urease-positive gram-negative organism adapted to gastric mucus.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Helicobacter pylori?
cards.back: Chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma, and gastric MALT lymphoma associations.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Bacteroides fragilis?
cards.back: Anaerobic gram-negative intestinal organism with a capsule that promotes abscess formation.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Bacteroides fragilis?
cards.back: Intra-abdominal abscesses after disruption of the gastrointestinal barrier.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Fusobacterium necrophorum?
cards.back: Anaerobic gram-negative rod found in the oropharyngeal region.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Fusobacterium necrophorum?
cards.back: Lemierre syndrome: septic internal jugular thrombophlebitis following an oropharyngeal infection.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Pasteurella multocida?
cards.back: Gram-negative coccobacillus carried by many cats and dogs.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Pasteurella multocida?
cards.back: Rapidly developing soft-tissue infection after an animal bite or scratch.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Francisella tularensis?
cards.back: Small intracellular gram-negative coccobacillus with a very low infectious dose.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Francisella tularensis?
cards.back: Tularemia, often after tick exposure or contact with infected animals.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Brucella species?
cards.back: Small intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli transmitted from animals or unpasteurized dairy.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Brucella species?
cards.back: Brucellosis, which may cause undulating fever and systemic illness.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Bartonella henselae?
cards.back: Gram-negative organism associated with cats and their fleas.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Bartonella henselae?
cards.back: Cat-scratch disease and bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Treponema pallidum?
cards.back: Thin spirochete that is poorly visualized by routine Gram stain.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Treponema pallidum?
cards.back: Syphilis, with primary, secondary, latent, and possible late manifestations.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Borrelia burgdorferi?
cards.back: Spirochete transmitted by Ixodes ticks.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Borrelia burgdorferi?
cards.back: Lyme disease, including erythema migrans, arthritis, carditis, and neurologic manifestations.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Borrelia recurrentis?
cards.back: Spirochete transmitted by the human body louse.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Borrelia recurrentis?
cards.back: Louse-borne relapsing fever due to antigenic variation.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Leptospira interrogans?
cards.back: Thin spirochete with hooked ends; transmitted through exposure to animal urine-contaminated water or soil.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Leptospira interrogans?
cards.back: Leptospirosis; severe disease may cause jaundice, renal injury, and hemorrhage.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Mycoplasma pneumoniae?
cards.back: Bacterium lacking a peptidoglycan cell wall and having sterols in its membrane.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Mycoplasma pneumoniae?
cards.back: Atypical pneumonia; cold agglutinins may occur but are not diagnostic by themselves.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Chlamydia trachomatis?
cards.back: Obligately intracellular bacterium with infectious elementary bodies and replicative reticulate bodies.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Chlamydia trachomatis?
cards.back: Trachoma, urogenital infection, neonatal conjunctivitis, and lymphogranuloma venereum, depending on serovar.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Chlamydia psittaci?
cards.back: Obligately intracellular bacterium associated with birds.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Chlamydia psittaci?
cards.back: Psittacosis, often an atypical pneumonia after bird exposure.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Rickettsia rickettsii?
cards.back: Tick-transmitted intracellular bacterium targeting vascular endothelium.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Rickettsia rickettsii?
cards.back: Rocky Mountain spotted fever; a rash may appear late or be absent early.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Coxiella burnetii?
cards.back: Intracellular bacterium often acquired by inhaling aerosols from infected livestock birth products.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Coxiella burnetii?
cards.back: Q fever, including acute febrile illness and persistent infection such as endocarditis.

cards.front: What laboratory or biological features characterize Ehrlichia chaffeensis?
cards.back: Tick-transmitted intracellular bacterium that forms morulae in monocytes.

cards.front: What diseases or clinical associations are characteristic of Ehrlichia chaffeensis?
cards.back: Ehrlichiosis, often with fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferases.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Herpes simplex virus 1?
cards.back: Enveloped double-stranded DNA virus; establishes latency in sensory ganglia, classically trigeminal ganglia.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Herpes simplex virus 1?
cards.back: Oral herpes and sporadic temporal-lobe encephalitis; it can also cause genital herpes.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Herpes simplex virus 2?
cards.back: Enveloped double-stranded DNA virus; establishes latency in sensory ganglia, often sacral ganglia.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Herpes simplex virus 2?
cards.back: Genital herpes, neonatal herpes, and recurrent aseptic meningitis are characteristic associations.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Varicella-zoster virus?
cards.back: Enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus that remains latent in sensory ganglia.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Varicella-zoster virus?
cards.back: Primary infection causes chickenpox; reactivation causes shingles.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Epstein-Barr virus?
cards.back: Enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus that infects B cells through CD21.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Epstein-Barr virus?
cards.back: Infectious mononucleosis and associations with several lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Cytomegalovirus?
cards.back: Enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus; infected cells may have large intranuclear inclusions.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Cytomegalovirus?
cards.back: Congenital infection and opportunistic retinitis, colitis, or other organ disease in immunocompromised hosts.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Human herpesvirus 6?
cards.back: Enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus, with HHV-6B a common cause of childhood primary infection.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Human herpesvirus 6?
cards.back: Roseola: high fever followed by rash as the fever resolves.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Human herpesvirus 8?
cards.back: Enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus also called Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Human herpesvirus 8?
cards.back: Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Adenovirus?
cards.back: Nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus with an icosahedral capsid.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Adenovirus?
cards.back: Respiratory illness, conjunctivitis, gastroenteritis, and hemorrhagic cystitis, depending on type.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Human papillomavirus?
cards.back: Nonenveloped circular double-stranded DNA virus; high-risk E6 and E7 proteins interfere with p53 and RB.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Human papillomavirus?
cards.back: Warts and, for high-risk types, anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Parvovirus B19?
cards.back: Small nonenveloped single-stranded DNA virus with tropism for erythroid precursor cells.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Parvovirus B19?
cards.back: Erythema infectiosum, transient aplastic crisis, and fetal hydrops.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Hepatitis B virus?
cards.back: Enveloped virus with partially double-stranded circular DNA; replication involves reverse transcription.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Hepatitis B virus?
cards.back: Acute or chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Hepatitis A virus?
cards.back: Nonenveloped positive-sense RNA virus usually transmitted by the fecal-oral route.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Hepatitis A virus?
cards.back: Acute hepatitis; it does not establish chronic hepatitis.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Hepatitis C virus?
cards.back: Enveloped positive-sense RNA virus with substantial genetic variability.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Hepatitis C virus?
cards.back: Often chronic hepatitis, with risks of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Hepatitis D virus?
cards.back: Defective enveloped RNA virus that requires hepatitis B surface antigen for its envelope.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Hepatitis D virus?
cards.back: Hepatitis in people coinfected with HBV or superinfected after chronic HBV infection.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Hepatitis E virus?
cards.back: Positive-sense RNA virus often transmitted enterically; zoonotic transmission also occurs.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Hepatitis E virus?
cards.back: Acute hepatitis that can be especially severe during pregnancy; chronic infection can occur in immunocompromised hosts.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Influenza A virus?
cards.back: Enveloped, segmented, negative-sense RNA virus with hemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface proteins.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Influenza A virus?
cards.back: Influenza; reassortment can generate major antigenic changes that contribute to pandemics.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Respiratory syncytial virus?
cards.back: Enveloped negative-sense RNA virus whose fusion protein promotes syncytium formation.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Respiratory syncytial virus?
cards.back: Bronchiolitis and pneumonia, especially in infants and older or vulnerable adults.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Measles virus?
cards.back: Enveloped negative-sense RNA virus spread efficiently through airborne transmission.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Measles virus?
cards.back: Measles with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and rash; rare late complication is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Mumps virus?
cards.back: Enveloped negative-sense RNA virus in the paramyxovirus family.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Mumps virus?
cards.back: Parotitis, orchitis, and aseptic meningitis.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Rubella virus?
cards.back: Enveloped positive-sense RNA virus.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Rubella virus?
cards.back: Usually mild rash illness; congenital infection can cause cataracts, hearing loss, and patent ductus arteriosus.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Rabies virus?
cards.back: Enveloped, bullet-shaped, negative-sense RNA virus that moves through peripheral nerves toward the central nervous system.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Rabies virus?
cards.back: Fatal encephalitis once clinical disease is established; exposure requires urgent evaluation before symptoms.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Poliovirus?
cards.back: Nonenveloped positive-sense RNA enterovirus transmitted mainly by the fecal-oral route.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Poliovirus?
cards.back: Usually asymptomatic infection; occasionally aseptic meningitis or asymmetric flaccid paralysis.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Rotavirus?
cards.back: Nonenveloped virus with a segmented double-stranded RNA genome.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Rotavirus?
cards.back: Gastroenteritis with watery diarrhea, particularly in young children.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Norovirus?
cards.back: Nonenveloped positive-sense RNA calicivirus with a low infectious dose.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Norovirus?
cards.back: Acute vomiting and diarrhea, often in outbreaks in shared settings.

cards.front: What genome or replication features characterize Human immunodeficiency virus?
cards.back: Enveloped retrovirus with reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease; infects CD4-bearing cells using coreceptors.

cards.front: What illness or complication is associated with Human immunodeficiency virus?
cards.back: Progressive immune dysfunction without effective control, leading to opportunistic infections and certain malignancies.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Candida albicans?
cards.back: Budding yeast that can form pseudohyphae and true hyphae; germ-tube formation is a classic laboratory clue.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Candida albicans?
cards.back: Thrush, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and invasive candidiasis in susceptible hosts.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Cryptococcus neoformans?
cards.back: Encapsulated yeast with narrow-based budding; capsular antigen can be detected in body fluids.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Cryptococcus neoformans?
cards.back: Meningitis and pulmonary infection, especially with impaired cell-mediated immunity.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Cryptococcus gattii?
cards.back: Encapsulated yeast in the Cryptococcus species complex associated with environmental exposure.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Cryptococcus gattii?
cards.back: Pulmonary and central nervous system cryptococcosis, including in some otherwise healthy hosts.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Aspergillus fumigatus?
cards.back: Septate hyphae with typically acute-angle branching.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Aspergillus fumigatus?
cards.back: Allergic bronchopulmonary disease, fungus balls in cavities, or angioinvasive disease in high-risk hosts.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Rhizopus species?
cards.back: Mucorales molds with broad, irregular, sparsely septate hyphae.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Rhizopus species?
cards.back: Mucormycosis, including rhino-orbital-cerebral infection in susceptible hosts such as those with diabetic ketoacidosis.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Histoplasma capsulatum?
cards.back: Thermally dimorphic fungus; small yeasts can be found within macrophages in tissue.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Histoplasma capsulatum?
cards.back: Pulmonary or disseminated histoplasmosis after environmental exposure, often to soil enriched by bird or bat droppings.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Blastomyces dermatitidis?
cards.back: Thermally dimorphic fungus with broad-based budding yeast in tissue.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Blastomyces dermatitidis?
cards.back: Pulmonary disease with possible dissemination to skin and bone.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Coccidioides species?
cards.back: Environmental molds forming spherules containing endospores in human tissue.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Coccidioides species?
cards.back: Coccidioidomycosis, often pulmonary, with possible dissemination including meningitis.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Paracoccidioides species?
cards.back: Thermally dimorphic fungi with multiple budding yeast forms, classically resembling a pilot wheel.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Paracoccidioides species?
cards.back: Paracoccidioidomycosis, including pulmonary and mucocutaneous disease in Latin America.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Sporothrix schenckii complex?
cards.back: Thermally dimorphic fungi; tissue yeast forms may be cigar-shaped.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Sporothrix schenckii complex?
cards.back: Nodules spreading along lymphatic channels after inoculation, including plant-related injuries or infected animal contact.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Pneumocystis jirovecii?
cards.back: An opportunistic fungus whose cyst forms can be highlighted with silver stains.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Pneumocystis jirovecii?
cards.back: Pneumonia with hypoxemia and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates in hosts with impaired immunity.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Malassezia species?
cards.back: Lipophilic yeasts; microscopy in pityriasis versicolor can show yeast clusters and short hyphae.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Malassezia species?
cards.back: Pityriasis versicolor with hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly patches.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Trichophyton species?
cards.back: Dermatophytes that digest keratin and can infect skin, hair, or nails.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Trichophyton species?
cards.back: Tinea infections such as athlete's foot and some scalp or nail infections.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Microsporum species?
cards.back: Dermatophytes classically infecting skin and hair.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Microsporum species?
cards.back: Tinea capitis and tinea corporis; some species fluoresce under a Wood lamp.

cards.front: What identifying feature is characteristic of Epidermophyton floccosum?
cards.back: Dermatophyte infecting skin and nails but typically not hair.

cards.front: What clinical disease is associated with Epidermophyton floccosum?
cards.back: Tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and some nail infections.

cards.front: How is Giardia duodenalis acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or through fecal-oral spread.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Giardia duodenalis?
cards.back: Small-intestinal infection causing malabsorption, bloating, and greasy diarrhea.

cards.front: How is Entamoeba histolytica acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of mature cysts through fecal contamination.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Entamoeba histolytica?
cards.back: Invasive colitis and liver abscess; trophozoites containing ingested red cells support identification.

cards.front: How is Cryptosporidium species acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of immediately infectious oocysts; routine chlorine levels may not reliably inactivate them.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Cryptosporidium species?
cards.back: Watery diarrhea, potentially persistent and severe in immunocompromised hosts.

cards.front: How is Cyclospora cayetanensis acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of sporulated oocysts, often on contaminated produce; freshly passed oocysts require environmental maturation.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Cyclospora cayetanensis?
cards.back: Prolonged or relapsing watery diarrhea.

cards.front: How is Trichomonas vaginalis acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Sexual transmission of trophozoites; there is no cyst stage.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Trichomonas vaginalis?
cards.back: Vaginitis or urethritis; many infections are asymptomatic.

cards.front: How is Toxoplasma gondii acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of tissue cysts in undercooked meat or oocysts from contaminated soil or food; transplacental transmission can occur.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Toxoplasma gondii?
cards.back: Congenital disease and reactivation encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts.

cards.front: How is Plasmodium falciparum acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Sporozoites introduced by an infected female Anopheles mosquito; no dormant hypnozoite stage.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Plasmodium falciparum?
cards.back: Malaria with potential for severe disease, including cerebral malaria and high parasitemia.

cards.front: How is Plasmodium vivax acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Anopheles transmission; dormant liver hypnozoites can persist.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Plasmodium vivax?
cards.back: Malaria with possible relapses from liver stages after blood-stage infection resolves.

cards.front: How is Babesia microti acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Usually transmitted by Ixodes ticks; transfusion transmission also occurs.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Babesia microti?
cards.back: Hemolytic illness; intraerythrocytic parasites may form a Maltese-cross pattern.

cards.front: How is Trypanosoma cruzi acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Commonly transmitted when infected triatomine-bug feces contaminate broken skin or mucosa.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Trypanosoma cruzi?
cards.back: Chagas disease, including dilated cardiomyopathy and gastrointestinal megasyndromes.

cards.front: How is Trypanosoma brucei acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Transmission through the bite of an infected tsetse fly.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Trypanosoma brucei?
cards.back: African trypanosomiasis with systemic illness and possible sleep disturbance and meningoencephalitis.

cards.front: How is Leishmania species acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Transmission by infected sand flies; amastigotes live in macrophages.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Leishmania species?
cards.back: Cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral leishmaniasis, depending on species and host factors.

cards.front: How is Enterobius vermicularis acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of eggs, with easy person-to-person spread and autoinoculation.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Enterobius vermicularis?
cards.back: Perianal itching, especially at night; eggs are collected using a perianal tape test.

cards.front: How is Ascaris lumbricoides acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of embryonated eggs from contaminated soil or food; larvae migrate through lungs.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Ascaris lumbricoides?
cards.back: Intestinal infection that can cause obstruction or biliary disease; lung migration can produce eosinophilic inflammation.

cards.front: How is Strongyloides stercoralis acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Filariform larvae penetrate skin; autoinfection permits persistence for decades.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Strongyloides stercoralis?
cards.back: Intestinal and skin symptoms; severe hyperinfection can occur with immunosuppression, particularly corticosteroid exposure.

cards.front: How is Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Hookworm larvae typically penetrate skin, migrate through lungs, and mature in the intestine.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus?
cards.back: Chronic intestinal blood loss leading to iron-deficiency anemia.

cards.front: How is Taenia solium acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Eating pork containing cysticerci causes an adult intestinal tapeworm; ingesting eggs causes cysticercosis.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Taenia solium?
cards.back: Taeniasis or tissue cysticercosis, including neurocysticercosis, depending on the ingested stage.

cards.front: How is Echinococcus granulosus complex acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Ingestion of eggs from infected canid feces.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Echinococcus granulosus complex?
cards.back: Hydatid cysts, often in liver or lungs; rupture can cause severe reactions and dissemination.

cards.front: How is Schistosoma species acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Freshwater cercariae penetrate skin; snails are intermediate hosts.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Schistosoma species?
cards.back: Egg-induced inflammation, including hepatointestinal disease or urinary disease depending on species.

cards.front: How is Trichinella spiralis acquired, and what life-cycle feature matters?
cards.back: Eating larvae in undercooked infected meat.

cards.front: What illness or finding is associated with Trichinella spiralis?
cards.back: Intestinal symptoms followed by muscle invasion, myalgia, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia.

cards.front: Which part of bacterial lipopolysaccharide mediates its major endotoxin activity?
cards.back: Lipid A, which can trigger innate immune signaling and systemic inflammation.

cards.front: What distinguishes transformation from bacterial conjugation?
cards.back: Transformation takes up free environmental DNA; conjugation transfers DNA through direct cell contact.

cards.front: What is bacterial transduction?
cards.back: Transfer of bacterial DNA between bacteria by a bacteriophage.

cards.front: Why do bacterial endospores matter clinically?
cards.back: They permit survival under harsh conditions and can resist many ordinary disinfection methods.

cards.front: What does a bacterial biofilm provide?
cards.back: An attached microbial community within a matrix that can enhance persistence on tissues or devices.

cards.front: What is the target of beta-lactam antibacterial drugs?
cards.back: Penicillin-binding proteins involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking during cell-wall synthesis.

cards.front: Why are beta-lactams ineffective against Mycoplasma on structural grounds?
cards.back: Mycoplasma lacks the peptidoglycan cell wall targeted by these drugs.

cards.front: How does diphtheria toxin inhibit protein synthesis?
cards.back: It ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, impairing translation.

cards.front: How does Shiga toxin impair protein synthesis?
cards.back: It damages 28S ribosomal RNA in the eukaryotic 60S ribosomal subunit.

cards.front: What is antigenic drift in influenza?
cards.back: Gradual antigenic change caused by accumulated mutations, especially in genes encoding surface proteins.
